silabus_tekst: NoSQL Database Technologies page 1 of 3 COURSE SYLLABUS NOSQL DATABASE TECHNOLOGIES Course syllabus for master's students specializing in Information Technology Level: Master's · 15 weeks · lectures, practical sessions, lab work NoSQL Database Technologies page 2 of 3 1. Course Overview This course gives a systematic understanding of non-relational (NoSQL) database management systems: the principles behind their design, the theoretical foundations of distributed data stores (the CAP theorem, the ACID/BASE consistency models), the four core data paradigms (key-value, document, wide-column, graph), and hands-on skills with the industrial-grade systems Redis, MongoDB, Apache Cassandra and Neo4j. The program follows the structure and content of courses taught at leading universities: CMU 15-445/645 “Database Systems” (data models, storage, transactions, distributed DBMS), MIT 6.830/6.5830 “Database Systems” (the NoSQL lecture, consistency/availability trade-offs), the University of Cambridge Part II “Databases” course (document and graph models, ACID/BASE/eventual consistency), and the IBM/edX “NoSQL Database Basics” program (hands-on work with MongoDB, Cassandra, Cloudant). The course runs for 15 weeks and combines lectures, practical (seminar) sessions and lab work in which every student completes assignments individually on real database systems. 2. Course Goals • build an understanding of the limits of the relational model when dealing with big data and high-load systems; • provide the theoretical foundation: the CAP theorem, the PACELC theorem, consistency models (strong, eventual, causal), ACID and BASE; • teach students to make an informed choice of NoSQL database type (key-value, document, wide- column, graph) for a given domain; • develop practical skills in schema design, querying and administering Redis, MongoDB, Cassandra and Neo4j; • develop the ability to design distributed storage: replication, sharding/partitioning, failure handling; • prepare students to independently design a polyglot-persistence architecture for a real project. 3. Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, students will be able to: • explains the CAP/PACELC theorems and justifies the choice of consistency model for a given scenario; • designs a denormalized document-database schema for given access patterns (query-driven design); • writes CRUD queries and aggregation pipelines in MongoDB, commands and data structures in Redis, CQL queries in Cassandra, and Cypher queries in Neo4j; • configures replication and evaluates read/write consistency levels in Cassandra; • designs and justifies a polyglot-persistence architecture for a course/capstone project. 4. Weekly Course Structure No. Topic Lecture, hrs Practice, hrs Lab, hrs 1 Introduction to NoSQL: from the relational model to distributed data stores 2 2 - 2 Data modeling for NoSQL (query-driven data modeling) 2 2 - 3 Redis I. The key-value model, data structures 2 - 2 NoSQL Database Technologies page 3 of 3 No. Topic Lecture, hrs Practice, hrs Lab, hrs 4 Redis II. Persistence, replication, Pub/Sub 2 - 2 5 Redis III. Usage patterns: caching, queues, rate limiting 2 2 2 6 MongoDB I. The document model, BSON, CRUD 2 - 2 7 MongoDB II. The Aggregation Framework, indexing 2 - 2 8 MongoDB III. Replication (replica set) and sharding 2 2 2 9 Cassandra I. The wide-column model, CQL, primary keys 2 - 2 10 Cassandra II. Replication, tunable consistency, anti-patterns 2 2 2 11 Neo4j I. The property graph model, the Cypher language 2 - 2 12 Neo4j II. Graph algorithms and applied use cases 2 2 2 13 Distributed systems: sharding, consensus (Raft/Paxos), fault tolerance 2 2 - 14 Polyglot persistence, NewSQL, search engines (Elasticsearch), choosing a technology 2 2 - 15 Final project defense, course review, exam preparation 1 3 - 5. Grading • Lab assignments (10 labs, submitted individually with a live demo) — 40% • Practical/seminar assignments and short written quizzes — 15% • Final project (designing a polyglot-persistence architecture + defense) — 30% • Written exam (theory: CAP/BASE, data models, consistency) — 15% 6. General Course References • Kleppmann M. Designing Data-Intensive Applications. — O'Reilly, 2017. • Sadalage P., Fowler M. NoSQL Distilled: A Brief Guide to the Emerging World of Polyglot Persistence. — Addison-Wesley, 2012. • Redmond E., Wilson J. R. Seven Databases in Seven Weeks. — Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018. • CMU 15-445/645 Intro to Database Systems — course materials and lecture recordings (Andy Pavlo), cmu-db.github.io / 15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu. • MIT 6.5830/6.830 Database Systems — OCW, ocw.mit.edu (the “NoSQL” lecture). • University of Cambridge, Computer Science Tripos Part II, “Databases” — cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching (sections Documents & Semi-Structured Data, Graph Databases). • IBM: NoSQL Database Basics (edX) — the four categories of NoSQL, hands-on practice with MongoDB, Cassandra, Cloudant. • Official documentation: redis.io/docs, mongodb.com/docs, cassandra.apache.org/doc, neo4j.com/docs.
